processing: Darjeeling orthodox black tea, best known in its light first flush form.
harvest_season: First flush in early spring is what the garden is famous for; later flushes follow through the season.
appearance_dry: Greenish, silvery twisted leaf in first flush; browner in later flushes.
appearance_liquor: Light gold in first flush, deepening to amber later.
taste_profile: Best known for first flush; as with other Darjeeling spring teas, expect floral, brisk notes, with more fruit in later pickings.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Spring lots turn sharp with boiling water, so cool it a little first.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush. First flush from the current year is the lot to look for, and it should be drunk fresh, ideally inside a year. Later flushes hold a bit longer, though this is not an ageing tea.
description:
Badamtam lies in the Lebong Valley, about 17 kilometres west of Darjeeling town, and runs down toward the Sikkim border. It is best known for its first flush tea, and it is a good name to know if spring Darjeeling is your thing.

The tea is made in the orthodox way, and as with other first flush lots it comes out light and green-looking. The later flushes are also made, though they carry less of the garden's name.

Brew it like a delicate tea rather than a breakfast one: cooler water, short steeps, no milk. If it tastes harsh, the water was too hot.

Buy current-year first flush from a seller who names the lot. The garden belongs to the Goodricke Group alongside Castleton and Thurbo, so it often appears in the same catalogues.
history: The garden was planted in 1858 by Christine Barnes before the Lebong Company took it commercial. It is now one of five Darjeeling estates owned by the Goodricke Group, with Thurbo, Barnesbeg, Castleton and Margaret's Hope.
